hooks.text: A one-hundred-twenty-five-million-dollar orbiter vanished because engineers forgot to convert units.
NASA lost an interplanetary probe not to a meteor, but to a unit mismatch.
One pound-force proved four point four five times stronger than a newton.

title: The Unit Mismatch That Cost NASA 125 Million
description: How a simple software mix-up between pound-force and newtons doomed the Mars Climate Orbiter in 1999.

beats.text: A one-hundred-twenty-five-million-dollar orbiter vanished because engineers forgot to convert units.
beats.visual: Mars Climate Orbiter artist concept by NASA, 1998

beats.text: After a nine-month journey, the Mars Climate Orbiter prepared for orbital insertion in September 1999.
beats.visual: Interplanetary trajectory diagram for Mars mission

beats.text: Communication with the probe was permanently lost as navigators searched for answers.
beats.visual: Jet Propulsion Laboratory mission control room, 1999

beats.text: An investigation revealed builder Lockheed Martin supplied impulse data in pound-force seconds.
beats.visual: Lockheed Martin Astronautics facility in Colorado

beats.text: Meanwhile, NASA's navigation software in California expected all incoming metrics in newton-seconds.
beats.visual: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory facility overview

beats.text: One pound-force is equal to four point four five newtons, multiplying small thruster forces into a fatal error.
beats.visual: LEROS bipropellant rocket engine test firing

beats.text: This mismatch plunged the spacecraft down to an altitude of only fifty-seven kilometers.
Surpassing eighty kilometers was the minimum survival altitude before the orbiter was destroyed.
beats.visual: Mars Polar Lander artist concept by NASA

beats.text: Engineers forgot simple unit conversions, meaning a one-hundred-twenty-five-million-dollar orbiter vanished.
beats.visual: Delta II 7425 launch of Mars Climate Orbiter, 1998
